input:
In this example, we will calculate the partial pressure of hexane above an ideal liquid mixture of hexane in heptane at the mixture temperature.

The liquid mole fraction $x$ of hexane, which is the volatile component of the pair, is 0.54. The pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ of hexane at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa. For an ideal solution, Raoult's law states that the partial pressure of a component over the liquid is equal to its mole fraction in the liquid multiplied by its pure-component vapour pressure at the same temperature, which can be written as follows:

$$p = x P^*$$

In this relation, $p$ denotes the partial pressure of hexane, $x$ denotes its liquid mole fraction, and $P^*$ denotes its pure-component vapour pressure. Substituting the values gives $p$ = 0.54 × 20.1 kPa = 10.9 kPa. As one would expect, the partial pressure comes out at a little over half of the pure-component vapour pressure: the mole fraction is itself a little over one half, and Raoult's law simply scales the vapour pressure by the mole fraction.

It should be emphasised that Raoult's law applies to an ideal solution, in which the interactions between unlike molecules correspond closely enough to those between like molecules for the mixture to follow the linear relation. Hexane in heptane comes close to this case, the two components being neighbouring hydrocarbons of similar size. The present calculation does not apply any activity coefficients. For the real mixture, an activity coefficient would be used to multiply the mole fraction and thereby correct the partial pressure for whatever departure from ideality is present; since no coefficient has been applied here, the value of 10.9 kPa stands as the ideal-solution value at the stated composition and temperature.
target:
Calculate the partial pressure of hexane over an ideal liquid mixture of hexane in heptane at the mixture temperature.

The liquid mole fraction $x$ of hexane, the volatile component, is 0.54. The pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ of hexane at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa. For an ideal solution, Raoult's law states that the partial pressure of a component over the liquid is its mole fraction in the liquid multiplied by its pure-component vapour pressure at the same temperature:

$$p = x P^*$$

In the relation, $p$ denotes the partial pressure of hexane, $x$ its liquid mole fraction, and $P^*$ its pure-component vapour pressure. Substitution gives $p$ = 0.54 × 20.1 kPa = 10.9 kPa. The partial pressure is a little over half the pure-component vapour pressure, as it must be: the mole fraction is a little over one half, and Raoult's law scales the vapour pressure by the mole fraction directly.

Raoult's law applies to an ideal solution, in which the interactions between unlike molecules match those between like molecules closely enough that the mixture follows the linear relation. Hexane in heptane is close to that case, the two being neighbouring hydrocarbons of similar size. The calculation applies no activity coefficients. For the real mixture, an activity coefficient would multiply the mole fraction and correct the partial pressure for what departure from ideality exists; no coefficient is applied here, so 10.9 kPa stands as the ideal-solution value at the stated composition and temperature. The same relation applied to heptane would require the heptane mole fraction and the pure-component vapour pressure of heptane, neither of which is stated, so no partial pressure for heptane is calculated. The stated value is a property of the liquid equilibrium at the mixture temperature: it does not depend on the volume of vapour standing over the liquid, only on the composition and the temperature.
